title: Inference economics suggestion notes
content:
Context and purpose:

This is a working memo for the Optimize team to consolidate recommendations that will feed into the inference cost models (spreadsheet referenced above) and the upcoming playbook. Goal: provide pragmatic, workload-driven defaults for batching, cache policy, and quantization that reduce per-token cost while keeping latency and quality risks explicit. This is an intermediate draft intended for engineering review; numbers are empirical-ish (pilot clusters + spreadsheet simulations) and will be validated in the next bench cycle.

Key constraints & assumptions used in the models:
- Target SLO buckets: interactive (p95 <= 200ms), nearline (p50 <= 500ms), throughput (best-effort latency).
- Typical request length distributions simulated: short (<=64 tokens), medium (65-512 tokens), long (>512 tokens).
- Baseline models in scope: modern 7B and 13B open families (representative inference costs from hosted runs).
- Hardware profiles: A100/RTX 6000 equivalent for dedicated pools; T4 in legacy regions for cost runs.
- Cache hit simulation assumes stable prefix reuse of 15–40% depending on product pattern.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Batch windows: 3–8ms micro-batching for interactive workloads; 25–75ms batching for nearline; aggressive 100–250ms for throughput jobs.
- Target batch sizes: prefer dynamic batching capped by token-constrained GPU occupancy rather than fixed count; aim for token-batch targets in simulation: 40k–80k tokens per device for seq lengths ~128. Translate to request counts per model via spreadsheet.
- KV/prefix caching: default prefix cache TTL 10m for interactive apps, 60m for product features with stable templates; enable mandatory small-object (<=1KB) cache for embeddings micro-services.
- Quantization: recommend two-tier profiles: safe (fp16 or nf4 with calibration) and aggressive (int8/awq for latency-sensitive, cost-optimized workloads) with automated rollback on eval drift.

Detailed recommendations

1) Batching and micro-batching settings
- Interactive (p95 <= 200ms):
  * Batching window: 3–8ms. This keeps responsiveness but allows some micro-merging to reach 5–15% token-cost savings for short-token flows.
  * Max batch token cap: 20k tokens per GPU for 7B-class, 30k tokens per GPU for 13B-class in interactive pools. Spreadsheet shows these caps reach ~75–85% occupancy on A100 for median request sizes.
  * Force early flush when queue latency > 75ms to preserve SLO.

- Nearline (p50 <= 500ms):
  * Batching window: 25–75ms. Prioritize throughput; this range gave 35–60% per-token cost reduction in sims.
  * Max batch token cap: 60k–120k tokens per GPU depending on seq length distribution and model. Use autoscaling to prevent excessive queuing.

- Throughput / offline jobs:
  * Batching window: 100–250ms. Aim for maximal GPU mem utilization and pipeline efficiency.
  * Consider persistent multi-query kernels / multi-sample micro-batching where model supports it.

Operational knobs and rationale:
- Prefer token-based caps over request-count caps: token variation is the main driver of GPU utilization. The spreadsheet shows request-based caps underutilize GPUs for mix with long sequences.
- Adaptive windowing: implement feedback where batching window shrinks if queue latency climbs; expands if occupancy drops below target.
- Backpressure policy: when queue depth indicates slowdown, route to lower-cost model variants or to dedicated burst lanes.

2) Caching (KV & prefix)
- Default TTLs:
  * Interactive chat templates / system prompts: 10 minutes. Rationale: template reuse is common but user behavior changes. 10m captures short-term reuse without large staleness risk.
  * Stable product templates (customer-provided prompt bundles): 60 minutes. For features with known repetitive invocations (e.g., email summary templates).
  * Embedding microservices: cache small embedding vectors (<=1KB) with TTL 24h when upstream semantics are stable; for dynamic data, fall back to 10m.

- Cache hit amplification techniques:
  * Prefix normalization: canonicalize whitespace, remove non-significant tokens in keys. Reduces key fragmentation significantly in pilot.
  * Shingled prefix keys for long prompts: store first-N tokens as a separate index to enable partial hits for long-tail.

- Cost vs staleness tradeoff: document expected cost savings in spreadsheet scenarios. Typical saving range: 12–45% token cost reduction depending on reuse rate and model family. Include regression test template to detect drift in quality when cached prefixes are used.

3) Quantization recommendation matrix
- Profile labels: safe, balanced, aggressive.
  * Safe: fp16 or bf16 when available — minimal quality risk, modest memory reduction. Use as default in hosted pools where high fidelity is required.
  * Balanced: nf4/4-bit quant with calibration and asymmetric rounding (when supported) — good tradeoff for most production workloads. Profile should include calibration step per-model and per-sequence-length bin.
  * Aggressive: int8/awq/4-bit post-training quant with activation folding — use for internal-only features or best-effort throughput tiers. Must be gated by automated eval checks (perplexity, task-specific metrics).

- Rollout rules:
  * Canary on 5–10% of traffic + automatic rollback if eval metric degrades >X% (tweak X per task; start with 2–4% for high-sensitivity tasks).
  * Keep a fallback path to compatible fp16 variant for each quantized model to allow immediate failover with minimal operational friction.

- Model-specific notes (examples):
  * M13-family (13B-class): Balanced quant (nf4) reduces memory footprint ~45% and reduced latency 20–35% in our bench. Aggressive int8 needs careful calibration for instruction-following tasks.
  * M7-family (7B-class): Aggressive quant often achieves >2x throughput improvement for embeddings and classification endpoints with low quality impact.

4) Spreadsheet controls and knobs to expose to customers and console
- Expose high-level presets: interactive/nearline/throughput with sliders for batch window and quantization profile.
- Advanced controls for platform admins: token-batch-target, max-batch-tokens, cache-ttl, prefix-normalization (on/off), quantization-profile (safe/balanced/aggressive).
- Provide estimated delta view in Console: show projected cost/savings and expected p95 change based on current traffic shape (pull from cost model sheet).

5) Validation plan and next steps
- Bench: run 3-week bench across representative workloads (search, chat, summarization) with A/B against baseline. Collect token-cost, p95/p50, and quality metrics.
- Spreadsheet updates: add columns for token-batch-target, simulated queue latency and projected cost per million tokens at each knob setting. Link provided in linked_artifacts.
- Evals: create small prompt set for each customer pattern to track quality regression per quantization profile and caching strategy.
- Rollout plan: staged canary, monitor model quality/eval, console exposure for operator override.

Open questions and risks (items to resolve during validation):
- How to price caching benefit to customers (we can present net per-token cost but need clarity on billing when cache reduces GPU usage).
- Exact rollback thresholds for different verticals; start conservative and tune.
- Operational complexity of maintaining two variants (quantized + fp16) for every model; consider automation to manage storage and warmup costs.

Appendix: quick knobs cheat sheet (for engineers)
- Interactive: window 3–8ms, max tokens/GPU 20k (7B) / 30k (13B), cache TTL 10m, default quant: safe.
- Nearline: window 25–75ms, max tokens/GPU 60k–120k, cache TTL 60m, default quant: balanced.
- Throughput: window 100–250ms, aggressive batching, cache TTL 60m+, quant: aggressive available.

Notes on spreadsheets referenced:
- The linked spreadsheet contains scenario tabs (short-only, mixed, long-heavy) and a sensitivity tab. When validating, please update the scenario with real production traces (we have export helpers in OPT-1173).

Call to action
- Feedback requested from serving-runtime and infra teams on feasibility of adaptive windowing prototype by EOD 2025-02-22.
- Product/Console: sketch quick UI for presets and projected-savings widget; sync by 2025-02-01.

Draft history: 2025-01-15 initial draft by Maya Patel; 2025-01-22 bench numbers added by Ethan Rivera; 2025-02-08 quantization notes updated by Leila Gomez.
